title: Structural biochemistry
description: Le domande dei Test A e B dell'anno scorso, più domande nuove sugli stessi argomenti. Ogni risposta ha la sua spiegazione.
description_en: Last year's Test A and B questions, plus new questions on the same topics. Every answer comes with an explanation.

A.question: Which four elements account for about 96% of the human body’s mass?
A.explanation: Oxygen, carbon, hydrogen and nitrogen make up about 96% of body mass; the others are present in much smaller amounts.
why: Calcium, sodium, potassium and chlorine are important but each is under 2% of body mass.
Iron, zinc, copper and manganese are trace elements: tiny amounts, though essential.
Sulfur, phosphorus, magnesium and calcium are present, but together they are only a few percent.
A.hook: CHON: the four letters of life. Remember them as one word.

A.question: The number of protons in an atom determines:
A.explanation: The atomic number (number of protons) defines which element an atom is; neutrons change the isotope, not the element.
why: The isotope depends on the number of neutrons, not protons.
Atomic radius depends on the electron shells and how strongly the nucleus pulls them.
Bonds are made by the outer electrons, not decided directly by the protons.
A.hook: Protons are the atom's ID card: 6 protons is always carbon, whatever else changes.

A.question: The quantum number n defines:
A.explanation: n is the principal quantum number: it sets the energy level (shell) of the orbital. Shape is l, orientation is ml, spin is ms.
why: Spin is the fourth quantum number, mₛ (+½ or −½).
Shape is set by l (s, p, d, f).
Orientation in space is set by mₗ.
A.hook: Think of an address: n = which floor, l = which kind of room, mₗ = which direction the room faces, mₛ = which of the two people inside.

A.question: Which rule states that two electrons cannot have the same set of four quantum numbers?
A.explanation: Pauli exclusion principle: no two electrons share all four quantum numbers, so an orbital holds at most two electrons with opposite spins.
why: Aufbau is about the order of filling: lowest energy first.
Hund's rule is about spreading electrons over orbitals of the same energy before pairing them.
Le Chatelier's principle is about chemical equilibrium, not electrons in atoms.
A.hook: Pauli = 'no two the same': at most two electrons per orbital, one spin up and one spin down.

A.question: Electronegativity represents:
options: The energy needed to remove an electron
The tendency of an atom to attract electrons in a bond
A.explanation: Electronegativity is the tendency to attract shared electrons in a bond. The energy needed to remove an electron is the ionization energy.
why: That is ionization energy.
Valence electrons are the outer electrons; electronegativity is how strongly an atom pulls on shared ones.
Isotopes differ in neutrons and have nothing to do with attracting electrons.
A.hook: Electronegativity is a tug of war over the shared electrons in a bond.

A.question: Carbon’s ability to form four covalent bonds is due to:
A.explanation: In the ground state carbon has only two unpaired electrons. One 2s electron moves to 2p, then the 2s and three 2p orbitals mix (sp³ hybridization) into four equal orbitals, one per bond.
why: Carbon has no d orbitals in its outer shell (only 2s and 2p).
Carbon's electronegativity is middling (2.5); it doesn't explain the number of bonds.
Carbon makes covalent bonds, not ionic ones.
A.hook: Like melting coins of different sizes into four identical coins: four equal orbitals, four equal bonds.

A.question: The ability of carbon to form long chains and complex branched molecules is mainly due to:
A.explanation: With four bonds available (tetravalence), carbon can bind other carbons in chains, branches and rings.
why: Low mass is not what lets atoms link into chains; the number of bonds is.
Carbon is only moderately electronegative; that's why it shares electrons instead of taking them.
Carbon doesn't form metallic bonds.
A.hook: Four hands: one to hold the previous carbon, one for the next, two left for branches.

A.question: Two molecules that are mirror, non-superimposable images are:
A.explanation: Enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images, like left and right hands. Epimers and diastereomers are not mirror images.
why: Epimers differ at only one chiral center and are not mirror images.
Diastereomers are exactly the stereoisomers that are NOT mirror images.
Geometric isomers (cis/trans) differ around a double bond or ring, not as mirror images.
A.hook: Enantiomers are your two hands: mirror images you can't stack on each other.

A.question: The α and β forms of glucose differ in:
options: Orientation of the hydroxyl on the anomeric carbon
A.explanation: When glucose closes into a ring, C1 (the anomeric carbon, the former C=O carbon) becomes a new chiral center. Its OH can end up below the ring (α) or above it (β): these two forms are anomers.
why: Both anomers have the same 6 carbons.
Ring closure doesn't change the oxidation state.
Glycosidic linkages join two sugars; α and β here describe a single glucose.
A.hook: α = OH down, β = OH up (Haworth). It matters: starch is α and we digest it, cellulose is β and we can't.

A.question: A pyranose ring in carbohydrates contains:
A.explanation: Pyranose = 6-membered ring like pyran: 5 carbons and 1 oxygen. A furanose ring has 5 atoms (4 C + 1 O).
why: Four carbons plus O would make a 5-membered ring (furanose).
The ring has 5 carbons, but you must count the oxygen too.
Seven-membered sugar rings are not the common forms.
A.hook: Pyranose: a hexagon, like the glucose ring. Furanose: a pentagon, like the fructose ring.

A.question: The main energy-storage polysaccharide in animals is:
A.explanation: Animals store glucose as glycogen, mainly in liver and muscle. Starch (amylose, amylopectin) is the plant equivalent.
why: Cellulose is a structural polysaccharide of plants, not a store.
Amylose is part of starch, the plant store.
Pectin is a plant cell-wall polysaccharide.
A.hook: Glycogen literally means 'sugar maker': the animal store. Starch is the plant version.

A.question: Cellulose differs from starch because:
options: It is made of fructose units
A.explanation: Cellulose uses β(1→4) links that keep the chain straight; starch uses α(1→4) links that make it bend into a helix.
why: Cellulose is linear, not branched.
α(1→4) is starch's link, not cellulose's.
Both are made of glucose.
A.hook: β keeps the chain straight like a beam, so cellulose makes rigid fibers; α bends it into a helix.

A.question: Lipids are generally characterized by:
A.explanation: Lipids are defined by their insolubility in water, not by a common structure.
why: The opposite: lipids are hydrophobic.
Peptide bonds are found in proteins.
Most lipids are neutral; only some (like gangliosides) carry charges.

A.question: Saturated fatty acids have:
A.explanation: Saturated means no C=C double bonds: the chain carries the maximum number of hydrogens.
why: One double bond = monounsaturated.
Several double bonds = polyunsaturated.
Fatty acids are linear chains, without rings.
A.hook: Saturated = 'full' of hydrogens: no room for double bonds.

A.question: The ω-3 and ω-6 fatty acids differ in:
options: Position of the first double bond from the methyl end
A.explanation: Omega (ω) is the last letter of the Greek alphabet, so it marks the last carbon (the methyl end). ω-3 means the first double bond starts at carbon 3 counting from that end; ω-6 at carbon 6.
why: Omega-3 and omega-6 can have similar lengths; the number refers to a position.
They are free fatty acids, the ester bond isn't what defines them.
Fatty acids don't contain phosphate.
A.hook: Omega = the end: count from the tail, not from the acid head.

A.question: Phospholipids are amphipathic molecules because they contain:
options: A polar head and nonpolar tails
A.explanation: Amphipathic means having a water-loving (polar, hydrophilic) part and a water-fearing (nonpolar, hydrophobic) part. In water the heads face outwards and the tails hide inside, forming a bilayer.
why: Phospholipids have one head, not two.
Then they couldn't face water on one side.
The tails are uncharged hydrocarbon chains.
A.hook: A matchstick: a polar head and a greasy stick. Two rows of matches tail to tail make a membrane.

A.question: In sphingolipids, the backbone is:
A.explanation: Sphingolipids are built on sphingosine, an amino alcohol, instead of glycerol.
why: Glycerol is the backbone of glycerophospholipids and triglycerides.
Cholesterol is a sterol, a different class.
The fatty acid is attached to the backbone, it isn't the backbone.

A.question: Cholesterol is essential for membranes because it:
A.explanation: Cholesterol slots between phospholipids, making the bilayer less fluid, more stable and a better barrier.
why: Hydrolyzing triglycerides is the job of lipases, not cholesterol.
Cholesterol is not an enzyme.
Peptide bonds are made by ribosomes.

A.question: Amino acids in proteins are:
A.explanation: Proteins are built from L-amino acids; sugars in nature are mostly D.
why: D is typical of natural sugars, not amino acids.
All amino acids except glycine have a chiral α carbon.
Living cells use only one form, not a mix.
A.hook: Amino acids L, sugars D: opposite hands.

A.question: The peptide bond is:
options: A partial double bond that restricts rotation
A.explanation: The electrons of the C=O and of the nitrogen are shared across the C–N bond (resonance), so it is halfway between single and double: shorter than a single bond, flat, and it can't rotate.
why: It's shorter and stronger than a single bond.
It's longer and weaker than a real double bond.
It is covalent, not ionic.
A.hook: A 'one and a half' bond: too double to rotate, too single to be a real double bond.

A.question: The α-helix is stabilized mainly by:
A.explanation: In the α-helix, the C=O of residue n bonds to the N–H of residue n+4: hydrogen bonds within the backbone.
why: Disulfide bonds link cysteines; they aren't what holds every helix.
Ionic bonds between side chains help little.
Van der Waals forces contribute, but the helix is defined by its H-bonds.
A.hook: Each C=O 'shakes hands' with the N–H four residues ahead (n → n+4).

A.question: In β-sheets, peptide chains are stabilized by:
A.explanation: β-sheets are held by hydrogen bonds between the backbone C=O and N–H of neighbouring strands, not by the side chains.
why: Side chains point above and below the sheet; the H-bonds are between backbones.
Hydrophobic effects drive folding in general, not the sheet's specific bonds.
Disulfide bridges are occasional, not the sheet's glue.

A.question: The Ramachandran plot shows:
options: Allowed φ and ψ angles in a polypeptide
A.explanation: Around each α carbon the backbone can rotate by two angles: φ (around N–Cα) and ψ (around Cα–C). The Ramachandran plot puts φ on one axis and ψ on the other, and shows which combinations are possible without atoms clashing. Each allowed region corresponds to a secondary structure.
why: DNA base pairing has nothing to do with it.
Enzyme rates are plotted with Michaelis-Menten curves.
Bond lengths are fixed values, not what the plot shows.
A.hook: A map with two angles: points in the α region make helices, points in the β region make sheets.

A.question: The quaternary structure of a protein refers to:
options: The folding of a single chain
A.explanation: Quaternary structure is how several polypeptide chains (subunits) assemble, as in hemoglobin's four chains.
why: Folding of one chain is tertiary structure.
Modifications aren't a level of structure.
Side chains are part of primary structure.
A.hook: Primary = sequence, secondary = local patterns, tertiary = one chain's 3D shape, quaternary = several chains together.

A.question: Collagen is composed of:
A.explanation: Each collagen chain is a left-handed helix (not an α-helix); three chains wind together in a right-handed triple helix.
why: Collagen chains are not α-helices: they're left-handed.
β-sheets are typical of β-keratin and silk.
Collagen is highly ordered.

A.question: The repeating amino acid motif in collagen is:
A.explanation: Gly-X-Y: glycine every third residue fits in the crowded centre of the triple helix; X and Y are often Pro and hydroxyproline.
why: That isn't collagen's repeat.
Leu, Ile, Val are hydrophobic residues with no special role in collagen.
Ser, Thr, Tyr are the phosphorylatable residues.
A.hook: Gly-X-Y, Gly-X-Y: glycine every third position, the only one small enough for the center.

A.question: Myoglobin’s main role is to:
A.explanation: Myoglobin is in muscle and stores O₂; its high affinity lets it hold oxygen until the muscle needs it.
why: CO₂ is carried mainly as bicarbonate and partly by hemoglobin.
Blood pH is buffered mainly by bicarbonate.
ATP is hydrolyzed by ATPases (e.g. myosin), not myoglobin.
A.hook: Myo = muscle: myoglobin is the muscle's oxygen tank, hemoglobin the delivery truck.

A.question: Hemoglobin’s sigmoidal oxygen-binding curve reflects:
A.explanation: A sigmoid (S-shaped) curve means cooperativity: the first O₂ binds with difficulty (T state, low affinity), but each bound O₂ makes the next ones easier, as the molecule shifts towards the R state (high affinity).
why: Constant affinity gives a hyperbola, like myoglobin.
Denaturation would destroy binding, not shape the curve.
Hemoglobin isn't an enzyme.
A.hook: The first guest is shy, then the party fills up fast: an S-shaped curve.

A.question: The Bohr effect describes:
options: Increased O₂ affinity at low pH
Decreased O₂ affinity at low pH
The binding of CO to hemoglobin
The oxidation of Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺
A.explanation: Bohr effect: lower pH (more H⁺ and CO₂, as in working muscle) lowers hemoglobin's O₂ affinity, so more O₂ is released.
why: The opposite: acid lowers affinity.
CO binding is CO poisoning, a different topic.
Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ gives methemoglobin.
A.hook: Working muscle is acidic and full of CO₂: hemoglobin lets go of O₂ exactly where it's needed.

A.question: Enzymes accelerate reactions by:
A.explanation: Enzymes lower the activation energy by stabilizing the transition state; they do not change the equilibrium.
why: The opposite: a higher barrier would slow the reaction.
Enzymes don't change the equilibrium, only how fast it's reached.
Enzymes act on substrates; they don't replace them.
A.hook: An enzyme digs a tunnel through the hill: same start and end, lower barrier.

A.question: Phosphorylation as a post-translational modification typically occurs on:
A.explanation: Only serine, threonine and tyrosine have the OH group on their side chain that kinases phosphorylate.
why: Gly, Ala, Leu have no –OH to phosphorylate.
Cys, Met, Trp have no –OH on the side chain.
Asp, Glu, His are not the classic phosphorylation sites.
A.hook: S-T-Y: the three amino acids with an –OH on the side chain.

B.question: Which subatomic particle carries a positive charge?
B.explanation: Protons are positive, electrons negative, neutrons neutral.
why: Electrons are negative.
Neutrons have no charge.
An isotope is a version of an element, not a particle.

B.question: The atomic number of an element corresponds to:
options: The number of electrons in a neutral atom
The sum of neutrons and protons
B.explanation: The atomic number is the number of protons. In a neutral atom the charges balance, so it also equals the number of electrons.
why: Neutrons give the mass number together with protons, not the atomic number.
Protons + neutrons is the mass number.
Valence electrons are only the outer ones.

B.question: Which orbital can hold a maximum of 10 electrons?
B.explanation: d sublevels have 5 orbitals × 2 electrons = 10. s holds 2, p 6, f 14.
why: s holds 2 (1 orbital).
p holds 6 (3 orbitals).
f holds 14 (7 orbitals).
B.hook: 1, 3, 5, 7 orbitals for s, p, d, f; double them: 2, 6, 10, 14. The periodic table has 2, 6, 10 and 14 columns in its blocks.

B.question: The tendency of an atom to attract shared electrons is called:
B.explanation: That is electronegativity. Ionization energy is the energy to remove an electron; electron affinity is the energy change when one is gained.
why: Ionization energy is the energy needed to remove an electron from an isolated atom.
Electron affinity is the energy change when an isolated atom gains an electron.
Polarization describes how a charge cloud gets distorted, not an atomic property scale.

B.question: Which statement about noble gases is correct?
options: They have complete outer electron shells and are chemically inert
They are the most reactive nonmetals.
B.explanation: Noble gases have a full outer shell, so they are very stable and hardly react (only Kr and Xe react, with F and O).
why: The opposite: noble gases have the highest ionization energies.
They hardly form bonds at all; only Kr and Xe react, and only with F or O.
Halogens are the reactive nonmetals; noble gases are the least reactive.
B.hook: Noble gases are 'full': a complete shell has no interest in giving or taking electrons.

B.question: Which property of carbon allows it to create the complex molecules essential for life?
options: It can form four stable covalent bonds in multiple arrangements
B.explanation: Four stable covalent bonds in many arrangements (chains, branches, rings, double bonds) give carbon its variety.
why: Carbon forms covalent bonds, not metallic ones.
Carbon neither loses nor gains electrons easily; it shares them.
Carbon is in group 14, not a noble gas.

B.question: The geometry of methane (CH₄) is:
B.explanation: Methane is sp³: four bonds pointing to the corners of a tetrahedron, at about 109.5°.
why: Planar geometry needs a double bond (sp²); methane has only single bonds.
Linear molecules have sp carbons (triple bond).
Trigonal planar is sp², as in ethylene.
B.hook: Single bonds = tetrahedron, double = flat, triple = line.

B.question: Molecules with the same formula but different spatial arrangements around a double bond are:
B.explanation: Different arrangements around a double bond (cis/trans or E/Z) are geometric isomers: the double bond does not rotate.
why: Enantiomers are mirror images around a chiral carbon, not around a double bond.
Conformers interconvert by rotation; a double bond can't rotate.
Epimers differ at one chiral center, typical of sugars.

B.question: A sugar containing six carbon atoms is called a:
B.explanation: Hexose = 6 carbons (glucose, fructose, galactose). Pentoses have 5, trioses 3.
why: Pentose = 5 carbons (e.g. ribose).
Triose = 3 carbons (glyceraldehyde).
Heptose = 7 carbons.
B.hook: Greek numbers: tri 3, pent 5, hex 6, hept 7.

B.question: The bond linking monosaccharides in disaccharides and polysaccharides is called a:
B.explanation: Monosaccharides are linked by glycosidic bonds; peptide bonds link amino acids, ester bonds are typical of lipids.
why: Peptide bonds link amino acids.
Ester bonds link fatty acids to glycerol.
Hydrogen bonds are weak interactions, not the links of a sugar chain.

B.question: The polysaccharide that forms plant cell walls is:
B.explanation: Cellulose, with β(1→4) links, forms the plant cell wall. Glycogen is the animal storage form.
why: Glycogen is the animal store.
Amylose is part of starch, a store.
Amylopectin is part of starch, a store.

B.question: The main function of carbohydrates in living organisms is to:
options: Serve as a primary source of energy
B.explanation: Carbohydrates are the main source of energy; DNA carries genetic information and lipids form membranes.
why: Genetic information is carried by nucleic acids (DNA, RNA).
Membranes are made mostly of lipids.
Catalysis is mostly done by enzymes, which are proteins.

B.question: Which of the following is not a lipid?
B.explanation: Glycogen is a polysaccharide (a carbohydrate), not a lipid.
why: Triglycerides are the classic storage lipid.
Phospholipids are membrane lipids.
Cholesterol is a sterol, a derived lipid.

B.question: Which type of fatty acid is liquid at room temperature?
B.explanation: Double bonds put kinks in the chain, so unsaturated fatty acids pack loosely and stay liquid (oils).
why: Saturated chains are straight and pack tightly: solid (butter).
Trans double bonds keep the chain straight, so trans fats are solid.
Very long chains raise the melting point.
B.hook: Olive oil (cis, unsaturated) stays liquid out of the fridge; butter (saturated) is solid in it.

B.question: The head group of a phospholipid is typically:
B.explanation: Phospholipid heads are polar and hydrophilic, facing the water on both sides of the bilayer.
why: The tails are nonpolar; the head is polar.
Heads are polar, often charged.
Hydrophobic describes the tails.

B.question: Which lipid component predominates in the myelin sheath?
B.explanation: Sphingomyelin is especially concentrated in the myelin sheath around nerve axons.
why: Cholesterol is abundant in myelin too, but the lipid typical of myelin is sphingomyelin.
Lecithin (phosphatidylcholine) is the common membrane phospholipid, not specific to myelin.
Triglycerides are energy stores, not membrane components.
B.hook: The name says it: sphingo-MYELIN is in the myelin.

B.question: The major structural difference between sphingolipids and phosphoglycerides is:
options: Sphingolipids contain sphingosine instead of glycerol
B.explanation: Sphingolipids have sphingosine as backbone instead of glycerol; both can carry phosphate.
why: Both can have saturated or unsaturated chains.
Sphingomyelin is a sphingolipid and has phosphate.
Sugars are typical of glycolipids, not of phosphoglycerides.

B.question: Which molecule serves as the precursor of all steroids?
B.explanation: Squalene, a triterpene built from isoprene units, is the precursor of cholesterol and therefore of steroids.
why: Palmitate is a fatty acid (C16).
Glycerol is the backbone of glycerides.
Stearate is a fatty acid (C18).
B.hook: Isoprene → squalene (shark liver oil) → cholesterol → all steroid hormones.

B.question: Which functional group is present in all amino acids?
B.explanation: Every amino acid has an amino group and a carboxyl group on the α carbon; they differ in the side chain.
why: Phosphate is not part of amino acids (it can be added by phosphorylation).
The carbonyl is part of the carboxyl, but 'amino and carboxyl' is the full answer.
Only some side chains (Ser, Thr, Tyr) have –OH.

B.question: Peptide bonds form between:
options: An amino and a carboxyl group
B.explanation: A peptide bond joins the carboxyl group of one amino acid to the amino group of the next, releasing water.
why: Two amino groups don't react with each other.
Two carboxyl groups don't form a peptide bond.
Side chains can link (disulfide), but that isn't a peptide bond.

B.question: The β-sheet is stabilized by:
B.explanation: β-sheets are held by hydrogen bonds between backbone atoms of adjacent strands.
why: Disulfide bridges aren't what holds β-sheets.
Ionic interactions are minor here.
Hydrophobic effects aren't the specific bonds of the sheet.

B.question: Which level of protein structure consists of simple, repetitive folding patterns such as α-helices and β- sheets?
B.explanation: Secondary structure means local repeating patterns of the backbone: α-helices and β-sheets.
why: Primary is the sequence.
Tertiary is the full 3D shape of a chain.
Quaternary is how chains associate.

B.question: A disulfide bond forms between two residues of:
B.explanation: Only cysteine has a thiol (–SH) group; two of them oxidize into a disulfide bridge.
why: Methionine contains sulfur but no –SH: it can't make disulfides.
Serine has –OH, not –SH.
Tyrosine has a phenolic –OH.
B.hook: Only cysteine has the –SH 'hook' that can clip to another one.

B.question: Which type of interaction mainly drives nonpolar amino acid side chains to the interior of a folded protein?
B.explanation: Hydrophobic interactions: nonpolar side chains gather inside, away from water.
why: H-bonds involve polar groups.
Ionic interactions involve charged groups.
Disulfides are covalent links between cysteines.
B.hook: Oil drops in water join together: same for nonpolar side chains inside a protein.

B.question: The basic structural unit of collagen is made of:
B.explanation: Tropocollagen, the basic unit, is three left-handed helices wound into a right-handed superhelix.
why: Two supercoiled α-helices is the coiled coil of α-keratin.
β-sheets aren't collagen's unit.
Collagen is fibrous, not made of globular subunits.

B.question: Collagen structure and stability depend largely on the presence of:
B.explanation: Glycine fits in the centre of the helix; proline and hydroxyproline are rigid and stabilize it.
why: Methionine and valine have no special role in collagen.
Glycine yes, but alanine isn't the key partner: proline is.
Lysine matters for cross-links, cysteine doesn't.

B.question: The prosthetic group of hemoglobin responsible for oxygen binding is:
B.explanation: Heme (protoporphyrin IX with Fe²⁺) binds O₂. NADH, FAD and biotin are coenzymes of other enzymes.
why: NADH is a coenzyme of redox enzymes.
FAD is the prosthetic group of flavoproteins.
Biotin is a coenzyme of carboxylases.

B.question: The oxygen dissociation curve of myoglobin is:
B.explanation: One chain, one binding site, no cooperativity: myoglobin's curve is hyperbolic.
why: Sigmoidal is hemoglobin (cooperative).
Binding saturates, so it can't be linear.
Not a real curve type here.
B.hook: One chain, one site: a simple hyperbola. Four chains talking to each other: an S.

B.question: The cooperative binding of oxygen in hemoglobin is explained by:
B.explanation: Cooperativity comes from the T (low affinity) to R (high affinity) transition as O₂ binds. The Bohr effect is a regulation by pH.
why: The Bohr effect is regulation by pH, not the source of cooperativity.
Fe³⁺ can't bind O₂ at all.
CO₂ transport is a separate job of hemoglobin.

B.question: Enzyme activity is generally lost at high temperature because:
B.explanation: Heat breaks the weak interactions holding the 3D structure: the enzyme denatures and the active site is lost.
why: Temperature doesn't change the amount of substrate.
pH and temperature are separate factors.
Cofactors aren't used up by heat.
B.hook: Like cooking an egg: the proteins unfold and don't come back.

B.question: An enzyme that moves a phosphate group from ATP to another molecule belongs to which class?
B.explanation: Moving a group (here phosphate) from one molecule to another is the job of transferases; kinases are transferases.
why: Hydrolases use water to break a bond.
Oxidoreductases move electrons.
Ligases join two molecules using ATP; here a group is moved.
B.hook: Kinases (like hexokinase, EC 2.7.1.1) are transferases: class 2.

N.question: Which quantum number defines the shape of an orbital?
N.explanation: The secondary (azimuthal) quantum number l sets the sublevel and the shape: l = 0 is s (sphere), l = 1 is p (two lobes).
why: mₗ gives the orientation, not the shape.
n gives the energy level (size).
mₛ is the electron's spin.

N.question: Hund's rule states that electrons in orbitals of the same sublevel:
options: Pair up as soon as possible
Occupy separate orbitals with parallel spins before pairing
N.explanation: Rule of maximum multiplicity: one electron per orbital, same spin, before any pairing. Carbon's two 2p electrons sit in separate orbitals.
why: Hund wants parallel (equal) spins first, not opposite.
The opposite: pairing is postponed until each orbital has one electron.
Filling goes from low to high energy (Aufbau).
N.hook: Bus seats: passengers take empty seats first, and only then sit next to someone.

N.question: The Aufbau principle states that electrons:
options: Cannot share all four quantum numbers
Fill orbitals in order of increasing energy
N.explanation: Aufbau means 'building up': lower-energy orbitals fill first. The other options describe Pauli and Hund.
why: That is Pauli's exclusion principle.
Parallel spins in separate orbitals is Hund's rule.
Electrons pair only when needed (Hund).
N.hook: Aufbau = building a house: you fill the ground floor before the upper ones.

N.question: How does ionization energy relate to atomic radius across the periodic table?
options: Both always increase down a group
N.explanation: Smaller atoms hold their electrons more tightly, so ionization energy rises where the radius shrinks: opposite trends.
why: Radius increases going down, but ionization energy decreases going down.
They move in opposite directions.
They are closely linked: a farther electron is easier to remove.
N.hook: Big atom, loose electron, cheap to remove. Small atom, tight electron, expensive.

N.question: How many electrons can a p sublevel hold?
N.explanation: A p sublevel has three orbitals (mₗ = −1, 0, +1), each with two electrons: 6.
why: 10 is the d sublevel.
2 is the s sublevel.
14 is the f sublevel.

N.question: Which two quantities are combined in Mulliken's electronegativity?
N.explanation: Mulliken: χ = ½(Ei − Eae). Electronegativity depends both on how hard it is to remove an electron and how much energy is gained by adding one.
why: Radius and mass are not in Mulliken's formula.
Spin and valence electrons are not part of it.
Protons and neutrons are not part of it.
N.hook: Mulliken averages 'how hard to take an electron away' and 'how glad to receive one'.

N.question: The carbon atoms in ethylene (CH₂=CH₂) are hybridized:
N.explanation: A double bond means sp²: three hybrid orbitals (planar, 120°) plus one p orbital that forms the π bond.
why: Carbon in a molecule is always hybridized.
sp is for triple bonds (acetylene).
sp³ is for single bonds only (methane, ethane).

N.question: Acetylene (CH≡CH) has carbons with which hybridization and geometry?
N.explanation: A triple bond means sp hybridization: two hybrid orbitals at 180°, so the molecule is linear.
why: sp² carbons are trigonal planar, and they form double bonds.
That is ethylene, with a double bond.
That is methane, with single bonds.

N.question: Epimers are stereoisomers that:
options: Are mirror images of each other
Differ only around a double bond
Interconvert by rotating a single bond
Differ in configuration at only one chiral center
N.explanation: Epimers differ at exactly one chiral center (e.g. glucose and galactose at C4) and are not mirror images.
why: Mirror images are enantiomers.
Differences around a double bond are geometric (cis/trans) isomers.
Interconverting by rotation describes conformers.
N.hook: Epimer: one difference only. Glucose and galactose: same except carbon 4.

N.question: Anomers are:
options: Epimers at the anomeric (hemiacetal) carbon of a cyclic sugar
N.explanation: When the sugar closes into a ring, C1 becomes a new chiral center; the α and β forms are anomers.
why: Amino acid enantiomers are D and L forms, not anomers.
cis/trans in fatty acids are geometric isomers.
Chair and boat are conformers of a ring; anomers differ in configuration.
N.hook: Anomer = epimer at the carbon born when the ring closes (C1 of glucose). α: OH down, β: OH up.

N.question: Conformational isomers differ from configurational isomers because they:
options: Need bonds to break to interconvert
Interconvert by rotation around single bonds
N.explanation: Conformers (like the chair and boat forms) change into each other just by rotation; configurational isomers need bonds broken.
why: Being mirror images is about enantiomers, not conformers.
That describes configurational isomers.
All isomers have the same formula.

N.question: A chiral (stereogenic) carbon is a carbon:
N.explanation: Four different groups around the carbon make two non-superimposable mirror arrangements possible.
why: A double bond makes cis/trans isomers possible, not chirality.
Two identical hydrogens means it can't be chiral: you need four different groups.
Ring carbons can be chiral or not; being in a ring isn't the rule.
N.hook: Four different 'hands' around one carbon = chiral.

N.question: Naturally occurring sugars are mostly:
N.explanation: Sugars in nature are mostly D (OH of the last chiral carbon on the right in Fischer); amino acids are mostly L.
why: L is typical of natural amino acids, not sugars.
Racemic means 50:50 D and L; nature is selective.
Most sugars have several chiral centers.
N.hook: Sugars D, amino acids L: opposite 'hands'.

N.question: Fructose is classified as a:
N.explanation: Fructose has 6 carbons and a ketone group (C2): a ketohexose. Glucose is an aldohexose.
why: Fructose has 6 carbons, not 5.
Aldohexose is glucose: C=O on carbon 1.
Fructose is neither 5 carbons nor an aldose.
N.hook: Fructose: Ketone in the middle (C2). Glucose: aldehyde at the end (C1).

N.question: A furanose ring contains:
N.explanation: Furanose, like furan, is a 5-membered ring with one oxygen (fructose often takes this form). Pyranose is 6-membered.
why: That is a pyranose (6-membered).
Four-membered sugar rings don't occur.
You must count the oxygen too: 4 C + 1 O.

N.question: Branch points in amylopectin and glycogen are formed by:
N.explanation: The main chain uses α(1→4) links; each branch starts with an α(1→6) link.
why: β links are in cellulose; starch and glycogen branches are α.
α(1→4) forms the linear chain, not the branch.
β(1→4) is cellulose's chain link.
N.hook: The 1→6 link reaches out to the 'side arm' of the glucose (C6 is the CH₂OH sticking out): that's where a branch can start.

N.question: Compared with amylopectin, glycogen has:
N.explanation: Glycogen branches every 4–10 residues (amylopectin every 15–30): more chain ends, so glucose can be released faster.
why: Glycogen is highly branched.
Glycogen uses α bonds.
The opposite: glycogen's branches are shorter and more frequent.
N.hook: Glycogen is a dense bush, amylopectin a sparser tree.

N.question: Liver glycogen mainly serves to:
options: Keep blood glucose available between meals and during fasting
N.explanation: Liver glycogen releases glucose into the blood when food is not available, and runs out in 12–24 hours. Muscle glycogen fuels the muscle itself.
why: That's muscle glycogen; muscle keeps its glucose for itself.
Plant cell walls are cellulose.
Fatty acids are stored as triglycerides in adipose tissue.
N.hook: Liver = the body's glucose bank; muscle = its own fuel tank.

N.question: In the Haworth projection of α-D-glucopyranose, the OH on the anomeric carbon is:
options: In the plane of the ring
N.explanation: α: anomeric OH down (opposite to C6), β: up. In the Fischer–Tollens projection α is on the right.
why: Substituents point above or below the ring, not in its plane.
Every sugar ring has an OH on the anomeric carbon.
Above the ring is β.
N.hook: α = down, β = up.

N.question: Which change makes a fatty acid more fluid (lower melting point)?
N.explanation: More double bonds (kinks) and shorter chains reduce packing between chains: more fluid.
why: Without the carboxyl group it wouldn't be a fatty acid at all.
Longer and saturated chains pack better: higher melting point.
Both changes make it less fluid.
N.hook: Short and kinked chains can't stack: they flow.

N.question: A triglyceride is:
options: Glycerol esterified with three fatty acids
Three glycerols linked to a phosphate
N.explanation: Triacylglycerol: glycerol's three OH groups each form an ester with a fatty acid. It is the main energy store.
why: Sphingosine is the backbone of sphingolipids, not glycerides.
Cholesterol with fatty acids gives cholesterol esters.
That doesn't exist; phospholipids have one glycerol.
N.hook: TRI-glyceride: three fatty acids, each on one of glycerol's three OH.

N.question: Plasmalogens differ from phosphatidates because:
options: The chain at position 1 is linked by an ether bond
N.explanation: In phosphatidates both fatty acids are joined to glycerol by ester bonds (–COO–). In plasmalogens the chain at position 1 is joined by an ether bond (–O–), which makes them more stable, antioxidant and resistant to phospholipases.
why: Plasmalogens are phospholipids: they do have phosphate.
Sphingosine is the backbone of sphingolipids.
Sialic acid is in gangliosides.

N.question: During apoptosis, phosphatidylserine:
options: Moves to the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane
N.explanation: Normally PS sits in the inner leaflet; exposing it on the outside is an 'eat me' signal of a dying cell.
why: PS is not converted into cholesterol.
It is normally already in the inner leaflet; apoptosis moves it out.
It isn't degraded: it's exposed.
N.hook: PS on the outside = 'eat me' flag of a dying cell for macrophages.

N.question: Gangliosides are acidic glycosphingolipids because they contain:
options: One or more sialic acid (NANA) residues
N.explanation: Sialic acid (N-acetylneuraminic acid) carries a negative charge. Cerebrosides and globosides have no NANA and are neutral.
why: Free fatty acids aren't part of a ganglioside.
Gangliosides have no phosphate.
They contain several sugars, including NANA.
N.hook: Gangliosides = Glycolipids with sialic acid, the 'acid' ones. Cerebrosides and globosides are neutral.

N.question: A cerebroside is made of:
N.explanation: Cerebroside = ceramide + a single sugar (galactose or glucose). With phosphocholine it would be sphingomyelin.
why: Ceramide + phosphocholine is sphingomyelin.
That is a diacylglycerol.
That is a ganglioside.
N.hook: Cerebroside: one sugar. Globoside: two or more neutral sugars. Ganglioside: sugars plus sialic acid.

N.question: Ceramide is formed by:
options: Sphingosine + a fatty acid linked by an amide bond
Two fatty acids linked by an ester bond
N.explanation: Ceramide is the core of all sphingolipids: sphingosine with a fatty acid attached through an amide bond.
why: Cholesterol + fatty acid is a cholesterol ester.
Glycerol + phosphate is the start of glycerophospholipids.
That is not a lipid class of the course.

N.question: The main role of brown adipose tissue is:
N.explanation: Brown fat cells are full of mitochondria (hence the colour) and burn lipids to produce heat. White fat stores energy.
why: Membranes aren't built by adipose tissue.
Long-term storage is white fat's job.
Cholesterol is made mainly by the liver.
N.hook: Brown fat is a radiator: many mitochondria burning fat into heat (newborns, cold).

N.question: How does cholesterol travel in the blood?
options: Bound to lipoproteins, mostly as cholesterol esters
N.explanation: Cholesterol is almost insoluble in water, so it travels in lipoproteins; about 65% is esterified.
why: Its solubility in water is far too low (0.2 mg/100 ml vs 160-240 mg/100 ml in blood).
Red blood cells carry oxygen, not cholesterol.
Hemoglobin binds O₂, CO₂ and H⁺, not cholesterol.

N.question: Where are sphingolipids mainly found in the plasma membrane?
N.explanation: The membrane is asymmetric: sphingolipids and plasmalogens face outside, PS and PI face inside.
why: They are membrane lipids, not cytoplasmic.
Membrane lipids are distributed asymmetrically.
The inner leaflet holds PS, PE and PI.
N.hook: Sugary and recognition lipids face outside, where other cells and pathogens can 'read' them.

N.question: Steroids such as cholesterol are built from:
N.explanation: Terpenes are polymers of isoprene; squalene (a triterpene) cyclizes into the four-ring sterane structure.
why: Glycerol is the backbone of glycerides.
Amino acids build proteins.
Glucose builds polysaccharides.

N.question: In an α-helix, how many residues are there per turn?
N.explanation: The α-helix is right-handed, with 3.6 residues per turn and H-bonds between residue n and n+4.
why: 2 is too few: that would be a flat zigzag.
10 is far too many.
4.5 is wrong; the H-bond goes to n+4, but there are 3.6 residues per turn.
N.hook: 3.6 residues per turn, bond to n+4.

N.question: Which amino acid is a strong α-helix breaker?
N.explanation: Proline's ring blocks rotation around the N–Cα bond and it lacks an N–H to donate an H-bond. Glycine also disfavours helices (too flexible).
why: Glutamate is common in helices.
Leucine favors helices.
Alanine is the best helix former.
N.hook: Proline is a kink: its ring locks the angle and it has no N–H to give.

N.question: In proteins, the peptide bond is mostly found in:
N.explanation: trans is more stable because it keeps the side chains apart. cis appears mainly before proline (about 5–10% of Pro).
why: The peptide bond can't rotate freely.
It's covalent, not ionic.
Cis is rare (mainly before proline).

N.question: Anfinsen's dogma states that:
options: Only enzymes have a native structure
The 3D structure is determined by the amino acid sequence
N.explanation: The native structure is the unique, stable, kinetically reachable free-energy minimum encoded by the sequence.
why: All proteins have a native structure.
Chaperones help, but the information is in the sequence.
Folding follows the sequence, not chance.
N.hook: The sequence is the recipe: Anfinsen's ribonuclease refolded alone in a test tube.

N.question: Which interaction stabilizing tertiary structure is covalent?
N.explanation: A disulfide bridge is a covalent bond between two cysteines; all the others are weak non-covalent interactions.
why: Hydrogen bonds are weak and non-covalent.
Hydrophobic interactions are non-covalent.
Van der Waals forces are non-covalent.

N.question: A holoprotein is made of:
options: A protein and a nucleic acid only
N.explanation: Conjugated protein: protein part (apoprotein) + non-protein part (prosthetic group), e.g. hemoglobin with heme.
why: Protein + nucleic acid is a ribonucleoprotein, not a holoprotein.
That's a homodimer.
Only amino acids = simple protein.
N.hook: Holo = whole: apoprotein + prosthetic group, like hemoglobin = globin + heme.

N.question: Levinthal's paradox points out that:
options: A protein cannot find its native structure by randomly trying every conformation
All proteins have the same fold
N.explanation: Trying every conformation would take longer than the age of the universe, so folding must follow guided pathways.
why: Proteins have very different folds.
Proteins do fold, and fast.
Folding is spontaneous; it doesn't need ATP.
N.hook: Trying every conformation would take longer than the age of the universe, yet proteins fold in milliseconds.

N.question: With the 20 standard amino acids, how many different tripeptides are possible?
N.explanation: 20 choices at each of 3 positions: 20³ = 8,000 (dipeptides: 20² = 400).
why: 400 is dipeptides (20²).
160,000 is tetrapeptides (20⁴).

N.question: A single collagen chain forms:
options: A left-handed helix with about 3.3 residues per turn
N.explanation: It is not an α-helix: each chain is left-handed; three of them wind into a right-handed superhelix.
why: Collagen chains aren't β-sheets.
Collagen chains are not α-helices.
They're very regular.

N.question: Why must every third residue of collagen be glycine?
options: It is small enough to fit inside the triple helix
N.explanation: The centre of the triple helix has room only for glycine's single H side chain.
why: Glycine has no –SH: only cysteine forms disulfides.
Glycine's side chain is uncharged.
Binding water is not its role.
N.hook: Only a single H can fit in the crowded core where the three chains meet.

N.question: A permanent wave (curling hair) works by rearranging which bonds in α-keratin?
N.explanation: Reducing and then re-oxidizing the disulfide bridges fixes a new shape. Washing and drying only rearranges hydrogen bonds (temporary).
why: Hydrogen bonds change with washing and drying: temporary.
Peptide bonds aren't broken by hair treatments.
Keratin has no glycosidic bonds.
N.hook: Water = temporary (H-bonds). Perm = permanent (disulfides).

N.question: β-keratin, found in feathers, scales and claws, is mainly made of:
N.explanation: β-keratin (reptiles, birds) is rich in β-sheets; α-keratin (mammals: hair, nails, skin) is made of α-helices.
why: Triple helices are collagen.
α-helices are α-keratin, in mammals.
Keratin is highly ordered.
N.hook: Birds and reptiles: β (beaks, feathers, scales). Mammals: α (hair, nails).

N.question: Collagen cross-links between chains start from:
N.explanation: Lysine is oxidized to allysine (an aldehyde), which reacts with Lys, OH-Lys or His to link chains together.
why: Glycine fills the helix core, it doesn't cross-link.
Collagen cross-links don't use cysteine disulfides.
Tryptophan isn't involved.

N.question: What does the hydroxylation of proline and lysine do in collagen?
options: Stabilizes the triple helix and enables cross-links and glycosylation
N.explanation: Hydroxyproline adds hydrogen bonds (also via water) that stabilize the triple helix; hydroxylysine allows glycosylation and cross-links.
why: It doesn't make it soluble; heating does (gelatin).
Collagen and keratin are different proteins.
It stabilizes the helix rather than breaking it.
N.hook: No vitamin C → no hydroxylation → weak collagen: scurvy (bleeding gums, poor wound healing).

N.question: Heating collagen produces:
N.explanation: Heat denatures the triple helix; on cooling, chains partly re-form helices randomly and trap water: a gel (gelatin).
why: Keratin is a different protein.
Elastin is a different protein.
Fibrin forms blood clots.
N.hook: Jelly sweets and broths: collagen from bones and skin, cooked into gelatin.

N.question: In functional hemoglobin, heme iron is:
N.explanation: Only Fe²⁺ binds O₂. Oxidized Fe³⁺ (methemoglobin) cannot carry oxygen.
why: Fe³⁺ is methemoglobin, which can't bind O₂.
Copper carries oxygen in some invertebrates (hemocyanin), not in hemoglobin.
Metallic iron (Fe⁰) isn't present in proteins.

N.question: The fifth coordination site of the heme iron is occupied by:
N.explanation: Four sites bind the porphyrin nitrogens, the fifth the proximal His of the protein; the sixth binds O₂ (empty in deoxy forms).
why: The distal histidine is on the other side and doesn't bind the iron.
Water isn't the fifth ligand.
O₂ takes the sixth site.
N.hook: Proximal = close (bound to the iron, below); distal = distant (above, near O₂, not bound).

N.question: The distal histidine lowers hemoglobin's affinity for CO because it:
options: Forces CO to bind at an angle
N.explanation: Free heme binds CO 25,000 times more than O₂; by forcing CO to bend, the distal His cuts that preference by about 100 times.
why: It doesn't bind CO itself; it gets in its way.
It doesn't react with CO.
Removing CO from the blood happens in the lungs.
N.hook: CO likes to bind straight; the distal His forces it to bend, so it binds less tightly.

N.question: 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG) in red blood cells:
options: Stabilizes the T state, lowering O₂ affinity
Stabilizes the R state, raising O₂ affinity
N.explanation: BPG holds hemoglobin in the T state so O₂ can be released in tissues. Fetal hemoglobin binds it poorly, so it has higher affinity.
why: The opposite: fetal hemoglobin binds it poorly.
Stabilizing R would raise affinity; BPG lowers it.
BPG binds in the central cavity between the β chains, not to iron.
N.hook: BPG is a wedge that keeps hemoglobin 'tense' (T), so it lets go of O₂. Without it, only 8% of O₂ would be released instead of 66%.

N.question: Deoxyhemoglobin is in which conformational state?
N.explanation: The T state is held together by 8 salt bridges between subunits; O₂ binding breaks them and shifts towards R.
why: Hemoglobin remains a tetramer.
It's a normal, working state.
R is the oxygenated form.
N.hook: T = Tense, Tight, Takes little O₂. R = Relaxed, Ready to bind.

N.question: Hemoglobin is made of:
options: Two α and two β chains (two αβ dimers)
N.explanation: Tetramer α₂β₂: two identical αβ dimers, each chain similar to myoglobin.
why: One chain is myoglobin.
Three helices is collagen.
There are two kinds of chain, α and β.

N.question: In red blood cells, CO₂ is mostly converted to bicarbonate by:
N.explanation: Carbonic anhydrase speeds up CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃ → HCO₃⁻ + H⁺; HCO₃⁻ leaves the cell in exchange for Cl⁻ (chloride shift).
why: Myoglobin stores O₂ in muscle.
Hemoglobin binds some CO₂, but the conversion is enzymatic.
2,3-BPG regulates O₂ affinity.

N.question: Compared with hemoglobin, myoglobin has:
N.explanation: Myoglobin is half-saturated at much lower O₂ pressure: it holds O₂ as a reserve, while hemoglobin must release it.
why: Both have heme.
Swapped: myoglobin's affinity is higher.
Their curves are very different.
N.hook: The tank (myoglobin) must hold on; the truck (hemoglobin) must unload.

N.question: Enzymes change which property of a reaction?
N.explanation: Enzymes speed up a reaction by lowering the activation energy; equilibrium and ΔG stay the same.
why: Equilibrium is unchanged.
Same products as without the enzyme.
ΔG is unchanged.

N.question: An enzyme catalyzes a reaction because it binds most tightly:
N.explanation: Binding the transition state more than the substrate lowers its energy. A protein that only binds the substrate tightly does not catalyze.
why: Binding the substrate too tightly would make the reaction harder, not easier.
Water isn't the key partner.
Holding on to the product would slow the enzyme down.
N.hook: The enzyme 'hugs' the halfway shape of the reaction, not the starting molecule.

N.question: An apoenzyme is:
options: The protein part alone, inactive without its cofactor
The active enzyme with its cofactor
N.explanation: Apoenzyme (protein only) is inactive; holoenzyme = apoenzyme + cofactor catalyzes.
why: A prosthetic group is the non-protein part.
Inhibitors are separate molecules.
That is the holoenzyme.
N.hook: Apo = 'away from': the cofactor is missing. Holo = whole.

N.question: In the induced-fit model:
options: The substrate is covalently modified first
The active site changes shape when the substrate binds
N.explanation: Lock-and-key assumes a rigid site; induced fit says both enzyme and substrate adjust when they bind.
why: An active site is always needed.
The substrate isn't modified before binding.
A rigid site is the lock-and-key model.
N.hook: Lock-and-key: rigid. Induced fit: like a glove that shapes itself around the hand.

N.question: Why do extreme pH values reduce enzyme activity?
options: They remove the active site's water
They change the charge of side chains and damage the 3D structure
N.explanation: At the optimal pH, acidic and basic residues have the right charge; away from it, the structure and the active site are altered.
why: pH and temperature are independent.
pH doesn't remove water.
pH doesn't add substrate.

N.question: An allosteric effector binds:
options: To a site other than the active site, changing the protein's shape
N.explanation: Allosteric = other site. Binding there changes conformation and so affinity or activity (2,3-BPG on hemoglobin is an example).
why: Allosteric binding is usually non-covalent and reversible.
It binds the protein, not the substrate.
If it bound the active site it wouldn't be allosteric.
N.hook: Allo-steric = 'other place'.

N.question: In Michaelis–Menten kinetics, at very high substrate concentration the rate:
N.explanation: When all active sites are busy (saturation), adding substrate no longer raises the rate: it approaches Vmax.
why: It doesn't drop: it levels off.
A rate can't be negative.
It slows down and flattens.
N.hook: Supermarket checkouts: past a certain number of customers the queue grows, but customers served per minute stay the same.

N.question: Compared with the whole atom (about 10⁻¹⁰ m), the nucleus (about 10⁻¹⁵ m) is:
N.explanation: 10⁻¹⁰ / 10⁻¹⁵ = 10⁵: the nucleus is about 100,000 times smaller, so the atom is almost entirely empty space.
why: It's the other way round: the nucleus is far smaller than the atom.
Atom and nucleus differ by five orders of magnitude.
N.hook: If the nucleus were a 30 cm ball, the outer electron would be 5.3 km away: farther than Pluto from the Sun at the same scale.

N.question: Of the 118 known elements, how many occur naturally?
N.explanation: 92 elements exist in nature; the other 26 were made in the laboratory and are often unstable.
why: 118 is the total, including the 26 made in the laboratory.
64 has no meaning here.
26 is the number of synthetic elements.
N.hook: 118 = 92 natural + 26 synthetic.

N.question: By mass, the most abundant element in the human body is:
N.explanation: Oxygen is about 65% of body mass, carbon about 18%, hydrogen about 9.5%: we are mostly water, and O is the heaviest atom in H₂O.
why: Hydrogen atoms are the most numerous, but they're so light they make only about 9.5% of the mass.
Carbon is second, about 18%.
Nitrogen is about 3%.
N.hook: We're mostly water, and in H₂O oxygen carries almost all the weight.

N.question: By type of molecule, the human body is made mostly of:
N.explanation: Water is about 62%, proteins and fats about 16% each, minerals 6%, carbohydrates only about 1%.
why: Fats are about 16%.
Proteins are about 16%.
Carbohydrates are only about 1%: we burn them rather than store them.

N.question: In the current (quantum) model of the atom, an orbital is:
options: The exact circular path of an electron
The fixed distance between two electrons
The space occupied by the nucleus
A region where the probability of finding the electron is high
N.explanation: Because of Heisenberg's uncertainty principle the electron's exact position can't be known; the orbital (from Schrödinger's wave function) describes where it is likely to be.
why: The planet-like orbit is the old model; we can't know the exact path (Heisenberg).
Orbitals describe one electron's probable position, not a distance between electrons.
The nucleus is in the middle; orbitals are around it.
N.hook: Not a track but a heat map of where the electron is likely to be.

N.question: The magnetic quantum number mₗ defines:
options: The energy level of the orbital
The orientation of the orbital in space
N.explanation: mₗ goes from −l to +l: for l = 1 it gives the three p orbitals along x, y and z. n gives the level, l the shape, mₛ the spin.
why: Shape is l.
Energy level is n.
Spin is mₛ.

N.question: The spin quantum number mₛ can take the values:
N.explanation: mₛ distinguishes the two electrons that can share one orbital: one +½, one −½.
why: Any positive integer describes n.
Those are the possible values of l for n = 3.
From −l to +l is mₗ.

N.question: How many electrons can the n = 3 level hold at most?
N.explanation: n = 3 has one 3s, three 3p and five 3d orbitals: 9 orbitals × 2 electrons = 18.
why: 8 is the 'octet' of s + p only; level 3 also has the d sublevel.
32 is the n = 4 level (it also has f).
10 is just the 3d sublevel.
N.hook: Maximum electrons in level n = 2n²: 2, 8, 18, 32.

N.question: Which describes the shape of s and p orbitals?
options: s has two lobes, p is spherical
s is spherical, p has two lobes
N.explanation: s orbitals are spheres that grow with n; p orbitals are bilobed; d and f have more complex shapes.
why: Swapped: s is the sphere.
Four lobes is typical of d orbitals.
Only s is spherical.

N.question: Why does the 4s sublevel fill before 3d?
options: 4s is closer to the nucleus than 3d
3d orbitals cannot hold electrons until period 5
N.explanation: Aufbau fills by increasing energy, and 4s is slightly lower than 3d. That's why the transition metals (filling 3d) sit in period 4.
why: 4s is actually farther out; what matters is its slightly lower energy.
3d fills in period 4, with the first transition metals.
Hund's rule is about spins within one sublevel, not the order of sublevels.
N.hook: 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d: the 4s 'jumps the queue'. That's why transition metals start in period 4.

N.question: Elements in the same column of the periodic table have:
options: The same configuration of outer (valence) electrons
The same number of electron shells
N.explanation: Chemistry is done by the outer electrons, so elements in the same group behave similarly. Along a row the number of outer electrons changes.
why: Atomic mass increases going down a column.
Elements in the same ROW have the same number of shells.
Each element has its own number of protons.
N.hook: Same column, same outer electrons, same chemical behavior: that's why the table is 'periodic'.

N.question: The d block of the periodic table contains:
N.explanation: Blocks follow the last sublevel being filled: s (first two columns), p (six right columns), d (transition metals), f (lanthanides and actinides).
why: Lanthanides and actinides are the f block.
Noble gases are at the far right, in the p block (helium in s).
Alkali metals are the first column, s block.

N.question: Atomic radius in the periodic table:
options: Depends only on the number of neutrons
Increases going up a group and to the right along a period
Increases going down a group and to the left along a period
Is the same for all elements of a period
N.explanation: Going down adds electron shells; going right adds protons that pull the same shell closer. Biggest atoms bottom-left (Cs), smallest top-right.
why: Neutrons don't affect the size of the electron cloud.
That is the direction of electronegativity and ionization energy, the opposite of radius.
Radius shrinks across a period as protons are added.
N.hook: Cesium (bottom left) is the biggest; fluorine and helium (top right) are tiny.

N.question: In successive ionization energies, a very large jump appears when:
options: The atom becomes a negative ion
The atom has an odd number of protons
The electron to be removed belongs to a complete inner shell
N.explanation: Each electron costs more than the previous one, but the big jump (lithium at the 2nd, beryllium at the 3rd) shows that a complete shell is very stable.
why: Removing electrons makes a positive ion, not a negative one.
The first electron is the cheapest one.
Odd or even proton numbers don't create the jump.
N.hook: Lithium: removing the 2nd electron means breaking into the complete 1s shell, so the cost explodes.

N.question: Which group has the highest electron affinity?
N.explanation: Halogens miss just one electron to complete their shell, so they gain one readily; noble gases are already complete.
why: Noble gases are already complete and don't want an extra electron.
Transition metals have middling values.
Alkali metals tend to lose electrons, not gain them.
N.hook: Halogens are one electron short of a full shell: they grab one gladly.

N.question: Electronegativity in the periodic table increases:
options: Up a group and to the right along a period
Down a group and to the left along a period
Only to the left along a period
N.explanation: Like ionization energy and electron affinity, it grows towards the top right (fluorine ≈ 4); atomic radius goes the opposite way.
why: Going down, outer electrons are farther away, so electronegativity decreases.
That's the direction of atomic radius, the opposite.
Going left it decreases.
N.hook: Top right is 'greedy' (fluorine ≈ 4), bottom left is 'generous' (cesium).

N.question: A bond between two atoms with a very large electronegativity difference (as in NaCl, Δ ≈ 2.2) is:
N.explanation: Δ = 0 gives a nonpolar covalent bond (O₂), a moderate Δ a polar covalent bond (HCl, Δ ≈ 1), a large Δ an ionic bond where one atom takes the electron.
why: Polar covalent needs a moderate difference, like HCl (about 1).
Nonpolar covalent needs nearly no difference, like O₂.
Metallic bonds join metal atoms, while NaCl has a metal and a nonmetal.
N.hook: A rope pulled by two people: equal force = nonpolar, one stronger = polar, one snatches the rope = ionic.

N.question: Krypton and xenon are noble gases, yet they can:
options: Bond with any element at room temperature
React with very electronegative elements such as F and O under special conditions
Lose electrons easily like alkali metals
N.explanation: Their outer electrons are far from the nucleus, so a very electronegative atom like fluorine can involve them: Xe + 3F₂ → XeF₆.
why: They react only with very electronegative elements, and only under special lab conditions.
Sodium is not electronegative enough to bond them.
Their ionization energies are high: they don't lose electrons easily.
N.hook: Xenon is big, so its outer electrons are far from the nucleus: fluorine, the greediest atom, can pull them into a bond.

N.question: Which statement about σ and π bonds is correct?
options: A σ bond allows rotation, a π bond blocks it
A π bond allows rotation, a σ bond blocks it
N.explanation: σ comes from head-on overlap along the axis and allows rotation; π comes from side overlap of unhybridized p orbitals and locks the bond.
why: π bonds block rotation.
σ bonds allow it.
Swapped: σ allows rotation, π blocks it.
N.hook: σ is a single rod along the axis, you can spin around it; π adds two side bars above and below that lock it.

N.question: A C=C double bond is made of:
options: One σ bond and two π bonds
One σ bond and one π bond
N.explanation: Double = 1σ + 1π (sp² carbons); triple = 1σ + 2π (sp carbons).
why: One σ + two π is a triple bond.
Every multiple bond has exactly one σ first.
Two atoms can share only one σ bond.

N.question: The bond that links fatty acids to glycerol in fats is formed by which functional group?
N.explanation: Alcohol + carboxylic acid → ester. Thiols are in cysteine, amines and amides in amino acids, aldehydes in aldoses.
why: Amines are in amino acids.
Thiols are in cysteine.
Aldehydes are in aldoses like glucose.
N.hook: Glycerol (an alcohol) + fatty acid (an acid) = ester: same reaction that makes the smell of fruit esters.

N.question: The thiol group (–SH), which can form disulfide bridges, is found in:
N.explanation: Two cysteine –SH groups can be oxidized to a –S–S– disulfide bridge, a covalent link in proteins.
why: Glycerol has –OH groups, no sulfur.
Glucose has –OH and C=O groups, no sulfur.
Cholesterol has one –OH and rings, no sulfur.
N.hook: Cysteine is the only amino acid whose side chain can bond covalently to another side chain: –S–S–.

N.question: Constitutional (structural) isomers differ in:
options: Only the spatial arrangement of the same connections
The order in which atoms are connected
N.explanation: Same formula, different connections. In stereoisomers the connections are the same and only the arrangement in space differs.
why: All isomers share the molecular formula.
Same connections in different spatial arrangement is stereoisomerism.
Rotation only gives conformers.
N.hook: Same LEGO bricks, built into different objects.

N.question: Diastereomers are stereoisomers that:
options: Are not mirror images of each other
Interconvert by rotation around single bonds
N.explanation: Geometric isomers (cis/trans) and epimers are diastereomers; enantiomers are the mirror-image ones.
why: That is the definition of enantiomers.
Rotation describes conformers.
Isomers always have the same formula.

N.question: Oleic acid and elaidic acid (both C18 with one double bond at C9) differ in:
options: Cis versus trans configuration of the double bond
N.explanation: Oleic acid is cis (chain bent by about 30°), elaidic acid is trans (nearly straight, like stearic acid, which is saturated).
why: Both have exactly one double bond.
Both are monounsaturated.
Both have 18 carbons.
N.hook: Oleic is in olive oil and is bent (cis); elaidic is the straight 'trans fat' version.

N.question: Mannose and galactose are epimers of glucose at, respectively:
N.explanation: Mannose differs from glucose only at carbon 2, galactose only at carbon 4.
why: Carbon 6 is the –CH₂OH, not a chiral center that differs here.
Swapped: mannose is C2, galactose is C4.
C1 differences give anomers, not mannose or galactose.
N.hook: Mannose is the near change (C2, right next to the aldehyde carbon); galactose the far one (C4).

N.question: In a Fischer projection:
options: Horizontal bonds point towards the viewer and vertical bonds away
The carbonyl group is always at the bottom
All bonds lie in the plane of the page
Vertical bonds point towards the viewer and horizontal bonds away
N.explanation: The tetrahedral carbon is rotated so the horizontal bonds come forward and the vertical ones go back; the aldehyde or ketone group goes at the top.
why: The carbonyl goes at the top.
That would be a flat molecule; a carbon with 4 bonds is tetrahedral.
Swapped: horizontal ones come forward.
N.hook: Fischer cross: horizontal arms hug you (towards you), vertical ones go away.

N.question: Whether a sugar is D or L is decided by:
options: Whether it is an aldose or a ketose
The OH on the chiral carbon farthest from the carbonyl (the penultimate carbon)
N.explanation: In the Fischer projection, OH on the right of the penultimate carbon = D, on the left = L, by comparison with D- and L-glyceraldehyde.
why: Both aldoses and ketoses come in D and L forms.
C1 is the carbonyl carbon (or the anomeric one in the ring).
Length doesn't decide D or L.
N.hook: Look at the second-to-last carbon: OH on the Right = D (Dexter, right).

N.question: The reference molecule for the ketose series is:
N.explanation: Aldoses derive from glyceraldehyde, ketoses from dihydroxyacetone, the simplest ketose.
why: Glucose is an aldohexose, not a reference.
Glyceraldehyde is the reference for aldoses.
Ribose is an aldopentose.

N.question: Glucose is classified as an:
N.explanation: Six carbons with the C=O on carbon 1 (aldehyde). Fructose, with the C=O on carbon 2, is a ketohexose.
why: Ketohexose is fructose.
Glucose has 6 carbons.
Glucose has 6 carbons.

N.question: Why is β-D-glucose the most stable monosaccharide?
options: In the chair conformation all its bulky groups are equatorial
N.explanation: Six-atom rings aren't flat: they fold into a chair or a boat. Each carbon then has an axial position (pointing up or down) and an equatorial one (pointing outwards). Bulky groups clash less when equatorial, and β-D-glucose is the only monosaccharide with all of them equatorial.
why: Glucose has several chiral centers.
It does form rings; most glucose in water is cyclic.
Rings with 109° angles fold; they aren't planar.
N.hook: All the bulky groups sit 'around the waist' (equatorial), none sticking up or down: no bumping.

N.question: An oligosaccharide contains:
N.explanation: Monosaccharides have 1 unit, oligosaccharides 2-10 (disaccharides are the main ones), polysaccharides more than 10.
why: They can contain different monomers.
One unit is a monosaccharide.
More than 10 units is a polysaccharide.

N.question: Lactose is made of:
N.explanation: Lactose (milk sugar) needs lactase to break its β bond; not all adults make it, hence lactose intolerance.
why: That is sucrose.
That is maltose.
That combination isn't a common disaccharide.
N.hook: Lactose = Lait (milk) = galactose + glucose; its β bond needs lactase.

N.question: Sucrose (table sugar) is made of:
N.explanation: Sucrose = glucose + fructose; lactose = galactose + glucose; maltose = glucose + glucose.
why: Galactose + glucose is lactose.
Glucose + glucose is maltose.
Not a common disaccharide.
N.hook: Table sugar (cane, beet) = glucose + fructose, the fruit sugar.

N.question: Maltose, produced by the digestion of starch, is made of:
N.explanation: Maltose is two glucoses linked α(1→4), the same bond found in the chains of starch.
why: Fructose dimers aren't the product of starch digestion.
That is sucrose.
That is lactose.
N.hook: Maltose comes from malt, i.e. from starch: two glucoses with starch's α(1→4) link.

N.question: A homopolysaccharide is:
options: A polysaccharide made of a single type of monomer
A polysaccharide made of two or more types of monomer
N.explanation: Starch, glycogen and cellulose are all homopolysaccharides of glucose; heteropolysaccharides contain two or more monomer types.
why: Cellulose is a homopolysaccharide and is linear.
That is a heteropolysaccharide.
Glycogen is an animal homopolysaccharide.

N.question: Starch is made of:
N.explanation: Two glucose polymers: mostly the branched amylopectin, with a smaller share of linear amylose.
why: Swapped: amylopectin is the majority.
Those are other polysaccharides; starch is amylose + amylopectin.
Starch contains both.
N.hook: Amylo-PECTIN is the Plentiful part (80-90%).

N.question: The structure of amylose is:
options: Linear β(1→4) chains forming straight fibers
Linear α(1→4) chain that coils into a left-handed helix of 6 glucoses per turn
N.explanation: The α(1→4) bond bends the chain, so amylose coils into a helix. Straight fibers are cellulose, with β(1→4) bonds.
why: That's cellulose.
Branched every 4-10 is glycogen.
Amylose is a long chain, not a small ring.

N.question: Muscle glycogen mainly serves to:
options: Supply quick energy to the muscle itself during intense effort
Keep blood glucose stable for the whole body
N.explanation: Muscle glycogen is fuel for the muscle and runs out in under an hour of intense effort; liver glycogen supplies the whole body and lasts 12-24 hours.
why: Fibers are made of proteins (actin, myosin).
That's liver glycogen.
Glycogen doesn't serve to store water.
N.hook: Muscle glycogen: about an hour of sprint. Liver glycogen: a day of fasting.

N.question: Why do cells store glucose as glycogen rather than as free glucose?
options: Glycogen is more soluble than glucose
Glucose is toxic in any amount
Free glucose cannot be used for energy
Many free glucose molecules would draw water into the cell; one large polymer does not
N.explanation: Osmotically, one big molecule counts as one particle. Its many branch ends also let enzymes add or remove glucose quickly, in parallel.
why: Glycogen is less osmotically active, not more soluble.
Glucose is the cell's normal fuel.
Free glucose is exactly what cells burn.
N.hook: A thousand loose marbles vs one bag of marbles: water 'counts' the loose ones.

N.question: In N-glycosylation, the sugar binds to:
options: The nitrogen of an asparagine side chain
The oxygen of a serine or threonine side chain
N.explanation: N-linked sugars (e.g. GlcNAc) attach to asparagine; O-linked sugars (e.g. GalNAc) attach to serine or threonine.
why: Cysteine sulfur forms disulfide bridges, not glycosylation sites.
That's O-glycosylation.
Sugars on lipids form glycolipids, not N-glycosylation.
N.hook: N-linked → asparagiNe (N is asparagine's one-letter code too). O-linked → the OH of serine or threonine.

N.question: Lipids are classified as simple, complex and derived. Which are derived lipids?
options: Steroids, sterols such as cholesterol, carotenoids
N.explanation: Simple: triglycerides and waxes. Complex (with an extra group): phospholipids and glycolipids. Derived: steroids, sterols, carotenoids.
why: Those are simple lipids.
Fatty acids are the building blocks of most lipids.
Those are complex lipids.

N.question: Palmitic acid has 16 carbons. By chain length it is a:
N.explanation: Short up to C5, medium C6-C12, long C13-C21, very long C22-C28.
why: Very long is C22-C28.
Medium is C6-C12.
Short is up to C5.

N.question: A monounsaturated fatty acid has:
N.explanation: Saturated: none. Monounsaturated (monoenoic): one. Polyunsaturated (polyenoic): two or more.
why: Fatty acids have double, not triple, bonds.
Two or more = polyunsaturated.
None = saturated.

N.question: How does a cis double bond affect a fatty acid chain?
options: It makes the fatty acid water-soluble
It bends the chain, so chains pack less tightly and the fat is more fluid
It keeps the chain straight, like a saturated one
N.explanation: Cis bends the chain by about 30°. Trans keeps it nearly straight, so trans fats pack like saturated ones and are solid.
why: Fatty acids stay hydrophobic.
The number of carbons doesn't change.
That's what a trans bond does.
N.hook: Cis = kink, trans = straight.

N.question: Brown adipocytes look dark because they contain:
N.explanation: Brown fat has small cells with many lipid droplets and many mitochondria; it produces heat. White fat has one big droplet per cell and stores energy.
why: Glycogen isn't what colors brown fat.
One big droplet is white fat.
Melanin colors skin, not fat.

N.question: Phosphatidic acid is made of:
options: Glycerol + fatty acids + a phosphate group
N.explanation: It is the backbone of the glycerophospholipids; adding a second alcohol to its phosphate gives the phosphatidates.
why: Cholesterol is a sterol.
Sphingosine is the backbone of sphingolipids.
That's a triglyceride.

N.question: The four alcohols that can be added to phosphatidic acid to form phosphatidates are:
N.explanation: They give phosphatidylethanolamine (PE), phosphatidylcholine (PC), phosphatidylserine (PS) and phosphatidylinositol (PI).
why: Ethanol and methanol aren't part of membrane lipids.
Glycerol and sphingosine are backbones, not head alcohols.
Sugars make glycolipids, not phosphatidates.
N.hook: E-C-S-I: Ethanolamine, Choline, Serine, Inositol → PE, PC, PS, PI.

N.question: In the plasma membrane, phosphatidylethanolamine and phosphatidylcholine are found mainly in:
options: Both only in the inner leaflet
Both only in the outer leaflet
PE in the inner leaflet, PC in the outer leaflet
PE in the outer leaflet, PC in the inner leaflet
N.explanation: Membrane lipids are asymmetric: PE, PS and PI mostly face the cytosol; PC, plasmalogens and sphingolipids mostly face outside.
why: PC prevails outside.
PE prevails inside.
Swapped.
N.hook: PC = Plasma membrane's Cover (outside); PE = Enclosed (inside).

N.question: Phosphatidylinositol is found mainly in the inner leaflet, where it is important for:
N.explanation: PI faces the cytosol and takes part in signaling; PS is the one flipped outwards during apoptosis.
why: That's PS, which flips out during apoptosis.
Myelin is rich in sphingomyelin.
Blood groups are globosides.

N.question: Thanks to their ether bond, plasmalogens:
options: Make membranes more fluid and less stable
Scavenge reactive oxygen species and resist phospholipases
Are more easily degraded by phospholipases
N.explanation: The ether bond gives antioxidant activity, more rigidity and stability (useful in nerves and heart) and resistance to phospholipases.
why: The ether bond makes them more rigid and stable.
They are part of membranes, mostly the outer leaflet.
The opposite: they resist phospholipases.

N.question: Globosides on red blood cells are:
options: The antigens of the ABO blood group system
N.explanation: Globosides are neutral glycosphingolipids with two or more sugars; their terminal sugars define the blood group.
why: Myelin is rich in sphingomyelin.
Those are gangliosides.
Cholera toxin binds a ganglioside (GM1).
N.hook: GLOBoside on GLOBules (red blood cells): your blood group.

N.question: Compared with groups A and B, the blood group O antigen:
options: Has no sugar chain at all
Has both the A and the B sugar
Has the base sugar chain without the extra terminal sugar
N.explanation: A adds an N-acetylgalactosamine, B adds a galactose, AB has both; O has only the base chain.
why: Group O still has the base chain.
That's group AB.
Sialic acid isn't part of ABO antigens.
N.hook: O = 'zero' extra sugar.

N.question: In ganglioside names such as GM1, GD3 or GT1, the second letter indicates:
options: The tissue where it is found
How many sialic acid (NANA) residues there are: M = 1, D = 2, T = 3
N.explanation: M, D, T = mono-, di-, trisialo. The number is 5 minus the count of non-NANA sugars.
why: Gangliosides have no phosphate.
The name doesn't describe the fatty acid.
The name isn't about tissues.
N.hook: M = Mono, D = Di, T = Tri sialic acids.

N.question: GM1 has 4 non-NANA sugars and GM2 has 3. Why is it called GM2?
options: 5 − 3 = 2: the number is 5 minus the count of non-NANA sugars
It was the second one discovered
N.explanation: Fewer neutral sugars means a higher number: GM1 (5 − 4), GM2 (5 − 3), GM3 (5 − 2).
why: The number isn't about fatty acids.
Not a discovery order.
Two sialic acids would be GD.
N.hook: Fewer sugars, bigger number: count backwards from 5.

N.question: Glycosphingolipids on the cell surface can act as:
options: Receptors used by toxins and pathogens, such as cholera toxin
N.explanation: Cholera, tetanus and botulinum toxins, bacteria such as E. coli and the influenza virus bind specific glycolipids.
why: Ion channels are proteins.
Fat digestion is done by lipases.
Energy stores are triglycerides and glycogen.

N.question: Sterane, the core of sterols, is made of:
options: A glycerol backbone and two fatty acids
Four fused rings: three with 6 carbons and one with 5
Six isoprene units in a chain
N.explanation: Squalene, a triterpene, cyclizes into the four-ring steroid core that becomes cholesterol.
why: That's a glyceride.
One of the four rings has 5 carbons.
Six isoprene units in a chain is squalene, the precursor.
N.hook: Steroid core: 6-6-6-5. Three hexagons and a pentagon.

N.question: Cholesterol in the plasma membrane:
options: Is found only in the inner leaflet
Increases the barrier effect and makes the membrane less fluid near the polar heads
N.explanation: Its rigid rings stiffen the chains near the heads, while the center stays more fluid: cholesterol regulates membrane fluidity.
why: It intercalates between phospholipids, it doesn't replace them.
It is in both leaflets.
It makes it less permeable: a better barrier.

N.question: Which amino acids have negatively charged (acidic) side chains?
N.explanation: Acidic: Asp, Glu. Basic (positive): Lys, Arg, His. Polar uncharged: Ser, Thr, Tyr, Asn, Gln. The rest are nonpolar.
why: Leucine and isoleucine are nonpolar.
Serine and threonine are polar but uncharged.
Lysine and arginine are positive (basic).
N.hook: 'Acid' is in their names: aspartic ACID, glutamic ACID.

N.question: In a folded globular protein, nonpolar side chains such as Leu, Val and Phe are mostly found:
options: Bound to the solvent by hydrogen bonds
In the interior, away from water
On the surface, in contact with water
N.explanation: Hydrophobic side chains cluster inside; polar and charged ones stay on the surface.
why: Nonpolar groups don't form H-bonds with water.
Polar and charged residues are on the surface.
Position in the sequence doesn't decide it.

N.question: Forming a peptide bond between two amino acids:
options: Requires adding a molecule of water (hydrolysis)
N.explanation: The carboxyl of one amino acid and the amino group of the next join with loss of H₂O. Breaking it is a hydrolysis.
why: Adding water breaks the bond (hydrolysis); forming it releases water.
Side chains aren't the ones joined.
No CO₂ is released.

N.question: The central dogma of biology describes the flow of information:
N.explanation: DNA is transcribed into RNA, which the ribosome translates into protein.
why: Information doesn't flow back from protein.
RNA → DNA happens only in retroviruses, not the dogma.
Protein is the end product, it doesn't make RNA.

N.question: In the genetic code, the codon AUG:
options: Codes for methionine and is the start codon
N.explanation: Every protein starts from AUG (Met). UAA, UAG and UGA are stop codons. Most amino acids have several codons: the code is redundant.
why: AUG is the most important codon of all.
Stop codons are UAA, UAG, UGA.
Glycine is GGx.
N.hook: AUG is the one 'go' signal (methionine); UAA, UAG and UGA are the three 'stop' signs.

N.question: Ferritin, casein and ovalbumin are examples of:
N.explanation: Storage: ferritin, casein, ovalbumin. Transport: hemoglobin, albumin. Contractile: actin, myosin. Structural: collagen, keratin.
why: Defense: immunoglobulins, complement.
Hormones: insulin, GH.
Contractile: actin, myosin.

N.question: Hemoglobin and myoglobin belong to which class of conjugated proteins?
N.explanation: Their prosthetic group is heme. Glycoproteins carry sugars (e.g. immunoglobulins), flavoproteins flavin nucleotides.
why: Lipoproteins carry lipids.
Glycoproteins carry sugars.
Flavoproteins carry flavin nucleotides.

N.question: Which peptide bonds are found in the cis form in about 5-10% of cases?
