N.explanation: Proline's nitrogen is closed in its ring, so cis and trans are similarly crowded. These cis bonds create kinks in the chain.
why: Cysteines form disulfides, not cis peptide bonds.
Glycine doesn't favor cis.
Peptide bonds in helices are trans.

N.question: The primary structure of insulin consists of:
options: Two chains (A and B) joined by disulfide bridges
A single chain with no disulfide bridges
N.explanation: Chain A has 21 amino acids and chain B 30, joined by two disulfide bridges (plus one inside chain A).
why: Triple helices are collagen.
Four subunits is hemoglobin.
Insulin has two chains and three disulfides.

N.question: The α-helix of proteins is:
options: Left-handed, with side chains pointing outwards
Right-handed, with side chains pointing inwards
Left-handed, with side chains pointing inwards
Right-handed, with side chains pointing outwards
N.explanation: Its handedness follows from L amino acids. Side chains point out, roughly perpendicular to the helix axis.
why: It's right-handed.
Side chains point outwards.
Both wrong.
N.hook: Right hand, thumb up along the axis: your fingers curl like the α-helix.

N.question: Which amino acids favor the α-helix?
N.explanation: Small hydrophobic residues fit the helix geometry well. Proline (rigid ring) and glycine (too flexible) break it.
why: Proline breaks helices.
Both break helices.
Glycine breaks helices.

N.question: Glycine destabilizes the α-helix because:
options: Its ring blocks the φ angle
Its side chain is just H, so it is too flexible and prefers other conformations
It has a charged side chain
N.explanation: In the helix propensity scale glycine costs about 4.6 kJ/mol more than alanine; proline is just as bad for a different reason (rigidity).
why: That's proline's ring.
Glycine has no sulfur.
Glycine's side chain is just H, uncharged.
N.hook: Proline too rigid, glycine too floppy: both bad for helices.

N.question: In an antiparallel β-sheet:
options: Adjacent strands run in opposite directions and the hydrogen bonds are straight
Strands are linked by disulfide bridges only
Adjacent strands run in the same direction
There are no hydrogen bonds between strands
N.explanation: Straight hydrogen bonds make antiparallel sheets usually more stable than parallel ones, where the bonds are angled.
why: Sheets are held by H-bonds, not disulfides.
That is a parallel sheet.
Sheets are made of H-bonds between strands.
N.hook: Anti-parallel = two lanes in opposite directions, with straight 'rungs' between them: more stable.

N.question: In a Ramachandran plot, glycine:
options: Has much wider allowed regions than other residues
N.explanation: With no side chain, glycine has few clashes and is the most flexible; proline, locked by its ring at φ ≈ −60°, is the most restricted.
why: It can be plotted like any residue.
It's the most flexible, not limited to helices.
Proline is the narrowest.

N.question: The empirical use of the Ramachandran plot is to:
options: Check the quality of an experimentally determined structure
N.explanation: Theoretical use: predict which φ/ψ angles are possible. Empirical use: compare observed angles with expected ones to spot errors.
why: The plot shows angles, not mass.
It doesn't predict sequences.
It doesn't count disulfides.
N.hook: Empirical = check real data: angles in forbidden regions flag errors in a solved structure.

N.question: A protein domain is:
options: A compact unit of secondary structure elements, often with its own function
N.explanation: Domains sit between secondary and tertiary structure and recur in different proteins, like reusable modules.
why: A complex of proteins is quaternary structure.
A single helix is secondary structure.
The sequence is primary structure.
N.hook: Like a reusable code module: the same domain turns up in different proteins.

N.question: In Anfinsen's experiment on ribonuclease:
options: The denatured enzyme refolded on its own and recovered activity
The enzyme needed chaperones to refold
The disulfide bridges re-formed at random
N.explanation: After denaturation, removing the denaturants let it refold and re-form the right 4 disulfide bridges out of 105 possible pairings: the sequence holds the information.
why: No chaperones: it refolded on its own.
The correct 4 out of 105 possible pairings re-formed.
It recovered its activity.

N.question: In the energy funnel of protein folding, the native structure is:
options: The global minimum of free energy
N.explanation: Unfolded forms are many and high in energy at the top of the funnel; the native state is one, at the bottom. Intermediates are local minima.
why: Local minima are intermediates where folding can get stuck.
The unfolded state is at the top.
The native state has the lowest energy.
N.hook: A funnel: many high-energy unfolded shapes at the rim, one native structure at the bottom. Like finding a global minimum in optimization.

N.question: In 2020, AlphaFold:
options: Predicted protein 3D structures from sequence with near-experimental accuracy
N.explanation: DeepMind's deep learning system solved a 50-year-old problem, measured at CASP14, a blind benchmark on unpublished structures.
why: Crystallography is experimental; AlphaFold is a deep learning model.
It predicts structures, it doesn't make molecules.
It is a prediction method, not an experiment on Levinthal.

N.question: Compared with globular proteins, fibrous proteins are generally:
N.explanation: Fibrous: insoluble, structural (keratin, collagen, elastin). Globular: soluble, functional (enzymes, hemoglobin).
why: Soluble and catalytic describes enzymes, which are globular.
That's globular proteins.
Catalytic proteins are globular.

N.question: In α-keratin, two α-helices wrap around each other to form:
N.explanation: Then two coiled coils form a protofilament and four protofilaments a filament, wound right-handed: alternating twists, like a rope.
why: Keratin is a twisted rope, not a straight rod.
β-sheets are β-keratin.
Triple helices are collagen.
N.hook: Like a rope: strands twisted one way, then bundled the other way, so it doesn't unravel.

N.question: Washing and drying hair changes its shape temporarily because:
options: Water breaks the hydrogen bonds between keratin chains, which re-form on drying
N.explanation: The change is temporary: the original shape is set by the stronger disulfide bridges, which only chemical treatments rearrange.
why: Water doesn't hydrolyze peptide bonds in hair.
Disulfides need chemicals (e.g. ammonium thioglycolate), not water.
Water doesn't add disulfides.
N.hook: Hair straightener: works until the next wash or humid day.

N.question: Collagen is synthesized by:
N.explanation: Fibroblasts in connective tissue, osteoblasts in bone, chondroblasts in cartilage. Keratin is made by keratinocytes.
why: Red blood cells make hemoglobin, not collagen.
Not only the liver: connective tissue, bone and cartilage.
Keratinocytes make keratin.
N.hook: Fibro-, osteo-, chondro-blasts: the 'builders' (-blast) of connective tissue, bone and cartilage.

N.question: Tropocollagen is made of:
options: Three left-handed chains supercoiled with a right-handed twist
N.explanation: Each chain is left-handed (about 3.3 residues per turn, not an α-helix); the three wind together the opposite way.
why: Collagen chains are left-handed, not α-helices.
Collagen has no β-sheets.
Three chains, not four.
N.hook: Three left-handed strands, twisted together to the right: opposite twists, like a rope.

N.question: Vitamin C deficiency weakens collagen because vitamin C is needed for:
options: The hydroxylation of proline and lysine
N.explanation: Without hydroxylation the triple helix is less stable and cross-links form poorly: this is scurvy.
why: Peptide bonds don't need vitamin C.
Glycine is made without vitamin C.
Secretion isn't the step that depends on it.
N.hook: Sailors without fresh fruit got scurvy: their collagen fell apart.

N.question: Two allysine residues from different collagen chains form which cross-link?
N.explanation: Allysine + lysine → lysinonorleucine (2 chains); allysine + allysine → allysine aldol (2 chains); aldol + His + OH-Lys → merodesmosine (4 chains).
why: Merodesmosine needs His and OH-Lys too, and joins 4 chains.
Collagen cross-links aren't disulfides.
Lysinonorleucine is allysine + lysine.

N.question: Which collagen cross-link joins four chains?
N.explanation: Merodesmosine forms from an allysine aldol plus a histidine and a hydroxylysine. More of these knots make collagen more mature and stronger.
why: Hydroxyproline is a modified residue, not a cross-link.
Lysinonorleucine joins 2 chains.
Allysine aldol joins 2 chains.
N.hook: Mero-DESMO-sine: desmos = bond, the biggest knot (4 chains).

N.question: Under the electron microscope, fibrillar collagen (e.g. type I) shows bands repeating every:
N.explanation: The staggered arrangement of molecules creates the D-period; fibers can reach 1 µm in diameter.
why: Ten times too large.
A thousand times too large.
Smaller than a single bond.
N.hook: D-period = 67 nm.

N.question: FACIT collagens:
options: Bind fibrillar collagen to other matrix molecules
Form large fibers on their own
N.explanation: Fibril-Associated Collagens with Interrupted Triple helices link fibrils to other proteins and glycosaminoglycans in the same tissue.
why: They are in many connective tissues.
That's type IV, a network collagen.
They don't form fibers on their own.
N.hook: FACIT = Fibril-Associated: they hang on the fibrils and connect them to the rest of the matrix.

N.question: Collagen type IV:
options: Forms the network of the basement membrane
Forms the thick fibers of tendons
N.explanation: Network-forming collagens (IV, VI, VIII, X, XXVIII) make meshes; type IV is the sheet that all epithelia rest on.
why: Type IV forms networks; FACIT collagens are IX, XII, XIV...
Tendons have fibrillar collagen (type I).
Collagen is extracellular.
N.hook: Type IV = the 'floor' (basement membrane) that epithelia stand on.

N.question: The heme group is:
options: Protoporphyrin IX with an Fe²⁺ ion at its center
A copper ion bound to histidines
A chain of four amino acids
N.explanation: Protoporphyrin IX is a tetrapyrrole; its four nitrogens hold the iron in the first four coordination sites.
why: Copper with histidines is hemocyanin, not heme.
Heme isn't made of amino acids.
Heme contains no sugar.

N.question: In deoxyhemoglobin, the sixth coordination site of the heme iron:
N.explanation: Sites 1-4: pyrrole N; site 5: proximal His; site 6: O₂ in the oxy form, empty in the deoxy form.
why: Pyrrole nitrogens take sites 1-4.
2,3-BPG binds the protein, not the iron.
The proximal His takes site 5.

N.question: The coordination bonds of Fe²⁺ in heme have which geometry?
N.explanation: Six ligands around the iron: four in the plane, one above and one below.
why: Linear is for 2 ligands.
Trigonal planar is for 3.
Tetrahedral is for 4.
N.hook: Six ligands = octahedron: four around the 'equator' (the porphyrin), one above, one below.

N.question: Regarding the spin state of the heme iron:
options: Deoxy forms are high-spin, oxy forms are low-spin
Spin does not change on O₂ binding
Deoxy forms are low-spin, oxy forms are high-spin
N.explanation: Binding O₂ splits the d orbitals more, so electrons pair in the lower ones (low spin). This is why spectra and blood color change.
why: They differ.
It changes; that's why the color changes.
Swapped.
N.hook: Deoxy = 'High' spin = dark venous blood; oxy = low spin = bright red arterial blood.

N.question: Methemoglobin:
options: Contains Fe³⁺ and cannot bind O₂
N.explanation: Outside the cell Fe²⁺ slowly oxidizes to Fe³⁺: old meat and dried blood turn brown.
why: Fetal hemoglobin is a normal, working variant.
Hemoglobin bound to CO is carboxyhemoglobin.
Oxygenated is oxyhemoglobin, with Fe²⁺.
N.hook: Brown meat and dried blood = Fe³⁺ = methemoglobin.

N.question: Why must O₂ not be released from heme as superoxide?
options: Superoxide is a reactive species that damages macromolecules, and leaves Fe³⁺ behind
N.explanation: Binding partly transfers an electron from Fe²⁺ to O₂. The protein stabilizes the complex so O₂ leaves intact and the iron stays ferrous.
why: That's not the issue; superoxide is a reactive oxygen species.
The problem is damage in the body, not breathing it out.
pH isn't the danger here.

N.question: When O₂ binds, what starts the conformational change of hemoglobin?
options: The iron moves into the porphyrin plane, pulling the proximal histidine and its helix
The heme detaches from the protein
N.explanation: The helix end sits at the dimer interface, so a movement under half an ångström spreads to the other subunits; the dimers rotate by 15°.
why: The chains stay together; the dimers rotate.
The heme stays bound.
Hemoglobin has no disulfide bridge involved here.
N.hook: A domino: iron moves (less than 0.5 Å), drags histidine, drags a helix, the dimers turn by 15°.

N.question: In the concerted (MWC) model of hemoglobin:
options: Subunits change one at a time as they bind O₂
Only the β subunits change state
All four subunits switch between T and R together
N.explanation: The sequential model instead has subunits change one by one, each easing the next. Both explain the sigmoid curve.
why: Both models have T and R.
That's the sequential model.
All subunits change.

N.question: Fetal hemoglobin has a higher O₂ affinity than maternal hemoglobin because it:
N.explanation: Less 2,3-BPG binding shifts its curve to the left, so O₂ passes from maternal to fetal blood across the placenta.
why: Fetal hemoglobin is a tetramer.
It has heme.
The opposite: it binds BPG less.
N.hook: The fetus 'steals' oxygen from the mother: its hemoglobin ignores BPG and holds O₂ more tightly.

N.question: In red blood cells, bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) leaves the cell:
N.explanation: CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃ (carbonic anhydrase) → HCO₃⁻ + H⁺. The H⁺ lowers Hb affinity (Bohr effect); HCO₃⁻ is exchanged for Cl⁻ (Hamburger phenomenon).
why: The exchange is with chloride, not sodium.
Bicarbonate travels in plasma, not on hemoglobin.
It leaves through a transporter, in exchange for Cl⁻.
N.hook: One out, one in: HCO₃⁻ out, Cl⁻ in. Charges stay balanced (Hamburger phenomenon).

N.question: At low pH, histidine 146 of hemoglobin:
options: Is protonated and forms a salt bridge with Asp 94, stabilizing the T state
Loses a proton and stabilizes the R state
Breaks the bond with the heme iron
N.explanation: Histidine changes charge near blood pH. One proton on one residue lowers the O₂ affinity of the whole protein.
why: At low pH it gains a proton and stabilizes T.
It doesn't touch the iron.
It doesn't bind O₂.
N.hook: Histidine is the pH sensor: it changes charge right around blood pH (7.4).

N.question: CO₂ that binds directly to hemoglobin (about 14%) attaches to:
options: The N-terminal amino groups, forming carbamates
N.explanation: The negative carbamate forms a new salt bridge with the other dimer, another way CO₂ stabilizes the T state.
why: That's where 2,3-BPG binds.
The iron binds O₂, not CO₂.
The distal His is near the O₂ site.

N.question: An enzyme that breaks a bond by adding a water molecule is a:
N.explanation: The six classes: oxidoreductases, transferases, hydrolases, lyases, isomerases, ligases (OTHLIL).
why: Oxidoreductases move electrons.
Isomerases rearrange a molecule.
Ligases join molecules using ATP.
N.hook: Hydro-lysis = water-splitting: amylase, peptidases and lipases are hydrolases.

N.question: An enzyme that joins two molecules using the energy of ATP is a:
N.explanation: Ligases (synthetases) use ATP; lyases (synthases) break or form bonds without water, oxidation or ATP.
why: Hydrolases break bonds with water.
Lyases form or break bonds without ATP.
Transferases move a group.
N.hook: LIgase = LInks with ATP. Lyase works without it.

N.question: An epimerase, which converts a molecule into one of its isomers, belongs to the:
N.explanation: Isomerases include epimerases and cis-trans isomerases; dehydrogenases and oxidases are oxidoreductases.
why: Oxidoreductases transfer electrons.
Transferases move groups between molecules.
Lyases form or break bonds.

N.question: The EC number of an enzyme (e.g. EC 2.7.1.1, hexokinase):
options: Has four parts: class, subclass, sub-subclass and the specific enzyme
Gives its optimal pH and temperature
N.explanation: Hierarchical like a folder path: 2 = transferase, 7 = transfers phosphate, 1 = to an alcohol group, 1 = hexokinase.
why: It doesn't count amino acids.
It doesn't give a mass.
It doesn't describe conditions.
N.hook: Like a folder path: class / subclass / sub-subclass / enzyme.

N.question: The active site of an enzyme is:
options: The site where allosteric effectors bind
The region where the substrate binds and the reaction takes place
The whole surface of the enzyme
N.explanation: Its shape and chemical environment let the enzyme recognize the substrate and make the reaction easier.
why: That's the allosteric site.
Position in the sequence isn't what defines it.
It's a small pocket, not the whole surface.

N.question: Trypsin cuts proteins only after lysine and arginine. This is an example of:
N.explanation: Absolute: one substrate (glucokinase). Group: substrates with a common group (trypsin). Bond: one bond type (α-amylase). Low: many substrates (CYP3A4).
why: Low specificity means many unrelated substrates (like CYP3A4).
Absolute means a single substrate (glucokinase).
Allostery is regulation, not specificity.

N.question: Km (the Michaelis constant) is:
options: The substrate concentration at which the rate is half of Vmax
The maximum rate of the reaction
N.explanation: Low Km means high affinity: the enzyme reaches half speed with little substrate.
why: At zero substrate the rate is zero.
Km is about substrate, not enzyme.
That is Vmax.
N.hook: Km = the 'half-speed' substrate concentration. Low Km = high affinity.

N.question: A competitive inhibitor:
options: Binds a different site and cannot be overcome by substrate
Binds the active site in place of the substrate, and can be overcome by adding more substrate
N.explanation: Non-competitive inhibitors bind elsewhere (to E or ES) and extra substrate does not help; uncompetitive ones bind only the ES complex.
why: That's an irreversible inactivator, not a competitive inhibitor.
That's non-competitive.
That's uncompetitive.
N.hook: Competitive = musical chairs: more substrate wins the chair back.

N.question: A coenzyme differs from a prosthetic group because the coenzyme:
options: Binds the enzyme with weak bonds and can detach
N.explanation: Coenzymes bind with weak bonds and can come off; prosthetic groups are bound covalently or very tightly and stay part of the enzyme. Many coenzymes derive from vitamins.
why: Cofactors are not proteins.
Many coenzymes come from vitamins.
That's a prosthetic group.

N.question: Glycogen phosphorylase is regulated by:
N.explanation: Phosphorylation (b ↔ a forms, driven by hormones) and allostery (T ↔ R, driven by the cell's energy state) combine into four activity levels.
why: Phosphorylation is only one of the two switches.
It's regulated on the spot, not only through gene expression.
Allostery is only one of the two switches.
N.hook: Two switches (hormones by phosphorylation, energy state by allostery): four levels, from 'really off' to 'really on'.
